item.description:

This video can not be playedFigure caption,
The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studioByHugh SchofieldIn ParisPublished19 minutes ago
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the White House press briefing room on Friday. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images

Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in BrusselsByRichard WheelerPolitical reporterPublished5 hours ago
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate
He got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.
The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.
“Who is he?” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China

item.title: [CBS News World] U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
item.description:
Tel Aviv — Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
President Trump also said this week that Iran may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, though he provided no evidence to support the claim.
Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions.
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.
The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind. The war was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in the recent midterm elections and it remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
The U.S. has significant firepower in the region, including tens of thousands of forces and two aircraft carriers with their associated strike groups, amounting to dozens of warships and aircraft.
For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

item.description:
Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as armed forces fight gangs to regain control of key corridor
Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regionsByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 19, 2026, 12:47 PM
Share
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armored vehicles rumbling through the community.
Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.

item.description:
Japan, India agree to enhance military and defense industry cooperation
Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drillsByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 19, 2026, 9:22 AM
TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan and India agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills, as their defense and foreign ministers met Thursday in Tokyo.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi joined their Indian counterparts, Rajnath Singh and S. Jaishankar, at the “two-plus-two" meeting in Tokyo.
The two Asian powers have been rapidly deepening security, defense and economic ties in recent years amid growing tension and uncertainty in the region. India and Japan also are part of the Quad grouping with the United States and Australia that aims to counter China’s influence.
“Through our cooperation, we hope to serve as the anchor for the Indo-Pacific region,” Motegi told a joint news conference after the talks.
This defense industrial cooperation will proceed under the framework of “design with Japan, make in India,” Singh said.
As an island nation with limited space to safely conduct missile tests and training, Japan needs defense partners that can provide facilities for its military to practice live-fire drills essential to improving missile capability. Japan struck a similar arrangement with Australia this year.

A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in OctoberByThe Associated PressNovember 19, 2026, 7:30 AM
Share
BRUSSELS -- A cyberattack carried out with artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, and some of the bloc's digital tools remain offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."

Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina correspondent , Reporting fromShenzhenPublished19 November 2026
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

View image in fullscreen
Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef
One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
